analysis.one_liner: Makes private equity funds liable for the debts of companies they buy and taxes fund managers' pay as ordinary income.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote in either chamber: it was referred to four House committees on introduction, sent to two Judiciary subcommittees a year later, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for private equity funds, the investment funds that buy controlling stakes in companies. It would make the fund and its investors legally liable for the debts, legal penalties, and pension shortfalls of companies they buy; ban the fund from paying itself dividends or buying back shares from an acquired company for two years; give workers' unpaid wages, severance, and benefits higher priority in bankruptcy; and close the carried interest loophole, which lets fund managers pay the lower capital-gains tax rate on their compensation [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies owned by private equity funds come out ahead if the bill passes. The bill's own findings say about 12 million people work for such companies, including workers at major retailers that went through bankruptcy like Sears, Toys 'R' Us, Payless, and Claire's [S3]. Those workers would see unpaid wages protected up to $20,000 (double the current cap), severance pay and health benefit contributions moved up the repayment line in bankruptcy, and limits on executive bonuses in bankruptcy cases [S3]. Employees and creditors would gain new tools to claw back money a fund stripped out of a company, with an eight-year window to challenge such transfers [S3]. Ordinary people who bought gift cards from a retailer that goes under would get up to $1,800 back ahead of other creditors [S3]. Pension funds and other investors in private equity would gain mandatory fee and return disclosures and fiduciary obligations from the funds they invest in [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at private-equity-owned companies and retail shoppers

how_it_helps.text: A private equity fund and its active investors would be jointly and severally liable for the debts, civil penalties, WARN Act liabilities, pension withdrawal liabilities, and pension insurance obligations of companies they acquire, so workers and government agencies could collect from the fund rather than only from an emptied-out subsidiary [S3].
An acquired company could not pay the fund dividends, buybacks, or similar payouts for two years after the takeover, and could not close a US plant to move jobs overseas during that window [S3].

In bankruptcy, the wage-priority cap would rise from $10,000 to $20,000, and severance pay and contributions to employee health plans would get priority status, putting workers ahead of general creditors [S3].
Courts could claw back transfers from an acquired company to the fund for up to eight years after a takeover, closing bankruptcy safe harbors that currently shield such payments [S3].
Carried interest, the fund managers' share of fund profits, would be taxed as ordinary income instead of at the lower capital-gains rate [S2] [S3].
Gift card holders would get a priority claim of up to $1,800 when a retailer they bought from goes bankrupt [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity fund managers and their investors pay. The liability rules, the two-year dividend ban, the surtax on payments from acquired companies, and the loss of the carried interest tax break all reduce the returns and shield protections the buyout industry currently has [S3]. Companies bought by funds would face tighter limits on interest deductions and would lose the ability to securitize risky corporate debt without keeping a slice of the risk themselves [S3]. A good-faith cost to weigh: funds that fear unlimited liability for everything an acquired company owes may decline to buy struggling companies at all, which could mean fewer rescues of failing businesses and potentially faster liquidations in some cases [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity fund managers and wealthy fund investors

drawbacks.text: Joint and several liability for every debt, penalty, and pension obligation of an acquired company is an expansive standard; funds could respond by avoiding acquisitions of companies with pension deficits or legal exposure, which may reduce the pool of buyers for struggling businesses [S3].

The bill bans post-acquisition dividends for two years but leaves the underlying leveraged-buyout structure intact; critics of buyouts argue the debt load itself, not just the payouts, is the problem, so the fix is partial [S3].

Stricter executive compensation rules in bankruptcy, including a requirement that bonuses be part of workforce-wide programs approved by a judge on clear and convincing evidence, could slow restructuring and give creditors another point of contention in a case where speed matters [S3].

The carried interest change raises the effective tax rate on fund managers' profit share, which by design reduces after-tax returns for the highest earners in the industry and modestly increases the cost of the investment management business [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete for a large group: roughly 12 million people work for private-equity-owned companies, and when those companies go bankrupt, workers currently stand near the back of the repayment line while funds have often already collected fees and dividends [S3]. The bill would flip that order and make the fund answerable for what the company owes. The main honest cost is that unlimited liability is a blunt tool: it could deter funds from buying distressed or pension-heavy companies, and the bill does not ban leveraged buyouts themselves, only their most visible side effects [S3]. On the whole the provisions directly target a documented pattern, the bankruptcies of major retailers owned by funds, and the costs fall overwhelmingly on fund managers and wealthy investors rather than on workers or the general public [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees on introduction, sent to two Judiciary subcommittees a year later, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the bill on October 20, 2021 with Reps. Jayapal, Norton, and Garcia of Illinois as original cosponsors; 16 Democrats in total cosponsored it, and no Republican did [S3] [S4].

On introduction it was referred to the Ways and Means, Financial Services, Judiciary, and Education and Labor Committees; none of them scheduled a markup, and there is no recorded committee vote or floor action in the bill's history [S5].
On November 1, 2022, the House Judiciary Committee referred the bill to two of its subcommittees, where it remained without further action [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died without ever coming to a vote in either chamber [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity fund managers and their investors came out ahead. They keep the current rules: liability limited to the money they put in, dividends and buybacks from acquired companies unrestricted, carried interest still taxed at capital-gains rates, and no new bankruptcy priority for workers' wages and severance [S2] [S3] [S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity fund managers and their investors

industries.note: The bill makes funds and their active investors liable for the debts and pension obligations of companies they buy, bars two years of dividends and buybacks from acquired firms, and taxes carried interest as ordinary income, cutting into the fee and profit streams that define the business model. Fund managers' gains often come from fees and payouts regardless of how the acquired company fares, which is exactly what the bill targets [S2] [S3].

Title VI would impose risk retention rules on securitizations of corporate debt, requiring lenders and securitizers to keep some of the risk they currently pass on to investors. These fees-and-pass-the-risk arrangements were flagged in the bill's findings as a source of systemic risk [S3].

Many pension funds invest in private equity, so tighter fund economics could affect their returns; but the bill deliberately exempts pension funds from the new liability rules and gives them fee, return, and fiduciary protections as investors. Their interest runs alongside the workers whose pensions they hold [S3].
